speaker: David Baker
title: Nobel Laureate David Baker on Using AI for Science to Solve Humanity's Biggest Problems
question: In biotech, how does a research institution outside major hubs like Boston or the Bay Area overcome venture capital centralization to build a local startup ecosystem?
guest: As we were able to design proteins that solve real problems, smart, ambitious people in my group would feel like, 'I designed this new protein to cure cancer—now I actually want to see whether it can.' To do that, you have to start a company; there's a limited amount you can do in an academic environment. So we developed a translational investigator program: after a graduate student or postdoc publishes their paper, they can transition into the program, where we raised philanthropic funding so they can develop the technology to the point where they can start a company and talk to VCs. We've spun out twenty-one companies now. When we first started, I talked to large VC firms and we never got past the second call because they always wanted the company in Boston, and I said it has to be in Seattle. Now it's completely changed—when we talk to VCs, they know it's going to be in Seattle. Every place has its own advantage: Seattle is very strong in AI and tech, and we have fantastic medical research organizations here, so the whole mentality around company formation has completely changed.

points.core: Academic labs hit structural limits that force researchers to spin out companies.
points.note: Accept: universities cannot take a published proof-of-concept molecule through clinical development, so ambitious trainees who want real-world medical impact must form startups. Do not credit: generic statements that startups make more money.

points.core: Philanthropy-funded translational fellowships mature academic discoveries into venture-ready biotech spinouts.
points.note: Accept: dedicated non-dilutive or philanthropic translational tracks let graduating PhDs or postdocs de-risk published research to the point where VCs will fund a company. Do not credit: vague suggestions to get more grant money.

points.core: Insisting spinouts stay local eventually flips venture firms from demanding relocation.
points.note: Accept: holding firm on keeping high-value spinouts in the home city—even if top VCs initially walk away—shifts investor norms once enough successful companies form there. Do not credit: generic advice to network with local investors.

points.core: Combining local AI tech talent with major medical institutes creates a regional advantage.
points.note: Accept: non-traditional biotech hubs succeed by pairing strong regional tech or AI density with existing clinical or biomedical research institutions rather than copying legacy hubs. Do not credit: generic claims about lower cost of living.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Institutions outside the major hubs generally succeed by substituting for the missing pieces of the venture stack themselves, rather than waiting for coastal investors to arrive.

The first step is filling the early funding gap with non-venture capital: university proof-of-concept and gap funds, evergreen or philanthropic seed funds, state matching programs, and heavy use of non-dilutive SBIR/STTR grants. This lets companies reach data milestones that make them credible to outside investors.

The second is importing or growing management talent, since experienced biotech executives are usually scarcer than money. Entrepreneur-in-residence programs, alumni networks, and partnerships with venture studios help here.

The third is building physical infrastructure, especially shared wet-lab incubators with affordable short-term leases, so startups have no reason to relocate.

Finally, they syndicate rather than compete: local seed money de-risks companies, then coastal VCs co-invest in later rounds, ideally without requiring a move. Focusing on a real institutional strength (as Pittsburgh, St. Louis, Madison, and Research Triangle have done) and recycling returns and experienced founders from early exits make the ecosystem self-sustaining over time. Expect this to take a decade or more.

The response treats staying local as a hoped-for outcome of syndication and omits how holding firm on location changes investor expectations over time.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: To overcome venture capital centralization, a research institution outside major hubs must de-risk discoveries internally before seeking coastal capital, since distant investors rarely fund raw academic science without relocating it. The institution first bridges the translational gap through internal proof-of-concept funds, affiliated seed vehicles, and non-dilutive grants—such as SBIR/STTR and state matching awards—to advance assets toward clear inflection points like preclinical validation or IND readiness. Simultaneously, it lowers startup capital intensity by providing turnkey wet-lab incubators, shared core facilities, and fast, founder-friendly technology licensing. Because VCs primarily relocate spinouts to access experienced management, the institution must also pair faculty inventors with seasoned entrepreneurs-in-residence and tap fractional or remote biotech executives. Finally, by cultivating co-investment syndicates with corporate pharma venture arms and coastal funds—while tying local seed capital, state incentives, and lower burn rates to a regional R&D presence—it keeps companies anchored locally until exits recycle talent and capital back into the ecosystem.

noweb.answer:
Research institutions outside major hubs overcome venture capital centralization by systematically de-risking science internally before seeking coastal capital and making local R&D too capital-efficient to relocate. Instead of spinning out raw academic IP, universities bridge the early funding gap with internal translational funds, disease-foundation philanthropy, and non-dilutive federal grants (such as SBIR/STTR) to reach decisive preclinical milestones that compel distant investors to engage. Many also establish dedicated university venture funds, state-backed matching vehicles, and strategic partnerships with pharmaceutical corporate venture arms to lead seed rounds and syndicate with coastal firms.

To keep funded startups from migrating, institutions lower early burn rates far below Boston or Bay Area levels by offering subsidized wet-lab incubators, access to expensive core facilities, and streamlined, founder-friendly licensing terms. Finally, because outside VCs hesitate most over local management depth, successful institutions run entrepreneur-in-residence programs and embrace hybrid leadership—pairing fractional or remote biotech executives situated near investors and pharma partners with scientific founders and lab teams anchored locally—until early exits begin recycling homegrown talent and capital back into the region.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
A research institution outside Boston or the Bay Area usually can't replace coastal venture capital, so the realistic goal is to bring companies far enough along that those investors will come in, while keeping a meaningful share of the work local.

The first step is getting capital in place before institutional VCs will invest. Successful regions have done this with evergreen seed funds tied to the institution (St. Louis's BioGenerator, UPMC Enterprises in Pittsburgh), state programs (Texas's CPRIT), and philanthropy. These sources pay for validation experiments that turn an academic finding into a project investors can fund.

The second step is importing operating talent. Programs like entrepreneurs-in-residence, venture-studio partnerships, and recruiting experienced executives give local science a credible team, which coastal funds care about as much as the technology.

The third step is making the institution easy to deal with: fast, standardized licensing terms, faculty incentives for founding companies, shared wet-lab incubator space, and access to core facilities and clinical-trial networks.

Finally, it works best to treat outside VCs as syndicate partners rather than competitors, and to accept hybrid companies that run R&D locally with leadership elsewhere. Strong clinical assets, lower costs and patient access can then help keep companies in the region over time.

noweb.answer:
A research institution can build a local biotech ecosystem by making it easier to start companies locally and bringing outside investors in early. It can fund proof-of-concept studies, offer predictable licensing terms and affordable shared lab space, and recruit experienced founders and operators to help researchers turn promising discoveries into companies. Local hospitals and industry partners can provide access to clinical expertise, validation, and early customers.

The institution can use grants, philanthropy, and regional seed funds to get startups to milestones that attract specialist venture firms. It can then build relationships with those firms before a financing round and connect them with local investors who can lead or co-invest. When founders and early employees go on to mentor, invest in, or start the next generation of companies, the region gains something that outside capital alone can’t provide: a growing pool of people who know how to build biotech companies locally.
